Currently, complete rodder trucks available on the market are oversized and overpriced to suit
the needs of the City. Maintenance staff require a smaller truck to navigate the narrow alleys and
roads in Encinitas. Since the chassis remains serviceable, a full replacement is not necessary at
this time and staff will continue to search for a suitable replacement specification to replace the
whole unit when the chassis reaches end of life. Staff recommends custom-building a new rodder
outfit on the existing chassis. AZ Wastewater Industries, Inc ( AWI), a vendor in Arizona, is
equipped to custom-build a rodder outfit according to the City’s requirements. The City’s
Purchasing and Contracts Policy allows for the use of sole source purchasing in extenuating
circumstances. In this case, AWI is the only reasonably known, capable supplier to fabricate and
install the rodder outfit, due to the unique nature of the WWC Division’s requirements, as well as
current market conditions.

Staff recommends pursuing a sole-source purchase through Municipal Maintenance Equipment
 MME) for the vacuum truck. Of all known vendors, MME is the only company able to provide the
type of vehicle that meets the City’s requirements. MME manufactures the Vac-Con, the only
combination cleaner with an auxiliary engine, while all other manufacturers provided single engine
units. The inclusion of an auxiliary engine is beneficial to Wastewater Operations due to the fuel
efficiency of the high-pressure water jet, which is used to clean sewer and storm drainpipes. With
the auxiliary engine, use of the high-pressure water jet requires approximately 100 horsepower,
while the single engine alternatives require one engine to run all equipment on the truck and use
approximately 400 horsepower to utilize their water jets. The auxiliary engine allows the truck’s
main engine to run fewer hours per day, which extends the maintenance and useful life of the
main engine and transmission. This also helps to reduce fuel consumption, greenhouse gases,
and maintenance and repair costs for the main engine. Staff will request and MME will offer a
trade-in value within six (6) months of delivery of the new unit. As the San Dieguito Water District
wishes to acquire the existing vehicle as a reserve for its emergency operations, the value
established by MME will set the market purchase price offered to SDWD. Proceeds from this
purchase will offset the final costs of the new Vac-Con. Moreover, the benefits extend even further
by serving as a reserve vehicle for emergency responses for storm mitigation and sewer overflow
events.

Each year, funds are appropriated in the budget to cover the replacement cost of heavy equipment
in the City’s fleet on a schedule that can vary. The Fleet Maintenance Division routinely monitors
service activity/costs and replacement needs and prepares a condition report for each piece of
heavy equipment. When possible, staff will attempt to extend the service life of the heavy
equipment. Although the budgeted replacement cycle for these two pieces of heavy equipment is
typically five (5) to seven (7) years, actual replacement needs can vary widely depending on its
use, driving conditions, current needs of the department, and other factors. These two assets are

After determining which equipment requires replacement, staff consults the protocol in the City’s
Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) Fleet Conversion Plan to select replacements. In the case of the
vacuum truck, there are currently no electric options available. A significantly more expensive fully
electric option exists for the rodder, but that option precludes the fiscally responsible reuse of the
existing chassis and is overpowered for the Wastewater Operations Division’s current operational
needs, so staff does not recommend the purchase of this electric alternative at this time. However,
both trucks will be fueled with renewable diesel. According to the Department of Energy
Alternative Fuels Data Center, “Life cycle analysis completed by Argonne National Laboratory
found that emissions for 100% biodiesel (B100) are 74% lower than those from petroleum diesel.
The California Air Resources Board has reported similar values for its life cycle analysis of
biodiesel from various sources.” (https://afdc.energy.gov/vehicles/diesels-emissions)

Currently, complete rodder trucks available on the market are oversized and overpriced to suit
the needs of the City. Maintenance staff require a smaller truck to navigate the narrow alleys and
roads in Encinitas. Since the chassis remains serviceable, a full replacement is not necessary at
this time and staff will continue to search for a suitable replacement specification to replace the
whole unit when the chassis reaches end of life. Staff recommends custom-building a new rodder
outfit on the existing chassis. AZ Wastewater Industries, Inc (AWI), a vendor in Arizona, is
equipped to custom-build a rodder outfit according to the City’s requirements. The City’s
Purchasing and Contracts Policy allows for the use of sole source purchasing in extenuating
circumstances. In this case, AWI is the only reasonably known, capable supplier to fabricate and
install the rodder outfit, due to the unique nature of the WWC Division’s requirements, as well as
current market conditions.

Staff recommends pursuing a sole-source purchase through Municipal Maintenance Equipment
(MME) for the vacuum truck. Of all known vendors, MME is the only company able to provide the
type of vehicle that meets the City’s requirements. MME manufactures the Vac-Con, the only
combination cleaner with an auxiliary engine, while all other manufacturers provided single engine
units. The inclusion of an auxiliary engine is beneficial to Wastewater Operations due to the fuel
efficiency of the high-pressure water jet, which is used to clean sewer and storm drainpipes. With
the auxiliary engine, use of the high-pressure water jet requires approximately 100 horsepower,
while the single engine alternatives require one engine to run all equipment on the truck and use
approximately 400 horsepower to utilize their water jets. The auxiliary engine allows the truck’s
main engine to run fewer hours per day, which extends the maintenance and useful life of the
main engine and transmission. This also helps to reduce fuel consumption, greenhouse gases,
and maintenance and repair costs for the main engine. Staff will request and MME will offer a
trade-in value within six (6) months of delivery of the new unit. As the San Dieguito Water District
wishes to acquire the existing vehicle as a reserve for its emergency operations, the value
established by MME will set the market purchase price offered to SDWD. Proceeds from this
purchase will offset the final costs of the new Vac-Con. Moreover, the benefits extend even further
by serving as a reserve vehicle for emergency responses for storm mitigation and sewer overflow
events.

SUBJECT:

Authorization to utilize PEG funding to upgrade the end-of-life audio-visual equipment in Council
Chambers, Carnation Conference Room, and Poinsettia Conference Room, project CT26A, in
order to integrate a 2-way audio-visual platform for public meetings in accordance with SB 707.


RECOMMENDED ACTION:

That City Council takes the following action:

   1. Approve upgrading the Council Chambers end-of-life audio-visual equipment & broadcast
       equipment with an audio-visual system that supports a 2-way audio-visual platform for
       public meetings in accordance with SB707 and the Americans With Disabilities Act; and

   2. Authorize the City Manager to enter a General Services Agreement between the City of
       Encinitas and Western Audio Visual, in conjunction with the City Attorney in substantial
       form as contained in Attachment 1. The cost to upgrade the audio-visual equipment is
       $197,663 for design, equipment, software, and installation. Staff is also requesting a 10
       percent contingency in the amount of $19,767 for a project total not to exceed $217,430.

   3. Adopt City Council Resolution 2025-113, titled “A Resolution of the City Council of the City
      of Encinitas, California, Amending the Fiscal Year 2025-26 Budget” (Attachment 2).

ENVIRONMENTAL CONSIDERATIONS:

The action being considered by the City Council is exempt from the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) because it is not a “project” under Section 15378(b)(5) of CEQA Guidelines.
The action involves an organizational or administrative activity of government that will not result
in the direct or indirect physical change in the environment.

This item does not relate to the Climate Action Plan.

GENERAL PLAN/CITY COUNCIL FOCUS AREAS:

This item is related to the Effective & Reliable City Services, Infrastructure, and Communications
focus area of the City Council Annual Work Plan.

FISCAL CONSIDERATIONS:

Staff recommends funding this project, CT26A – Council Chambers & Overflow AV Upgrades
from the Public, Education, and Government (PEG) Fees Fund. Total costs for the project are
expected to be $217,430.

The use of PEG Fees for this upgrade is appropriate, as these funds are specifically designated
for capital expenses related to public meeting broadcasts, ensuring compliance with SB 707 and
the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) (through enhanced closed captioning and accessibility).

This expenditure is considered a one-time capital improvement. Staff will incorporate any future
annual maintenance, software licensing, or subscription fees associated with the new equipment
into the subsequent fiscal year's operating budget for the Information Technology Department,
utilizing available PEG fees first if eligible.

Upgrades by room & function is as follows:

 Room/Function                                    Cost
 Broadcast equipment                              $79,010
 Council Chambers                                 $21,378
 Carnation                                        $32,261
 Poinsettia                                       $58,014
 Sales Tax                                        $7,000


The recommendation includes a 10 percent contingency of $19,767 to cover unforeseen costs,
change orders, or necessary modifications during installation. Any unspent contingency funds will
be returned to the PEG Fees Fund upon project completion.


BACKGROUND:

A/V equipment in the Council Chambers, Carnation Room, and Poinsettia Room was last
replaced in 2020, with some hardware approaching end of life in 2026. This technical
obsolescence requires immediate hardware replacement to maintain operational function.

The need for replacement is mandatory due to a legislative requirement established by Senate
Bill 707 (SB 707). This state mandate requires that, beginning July 2026, all open and public
meetings must include an opportunity for members of the public to attend and participate via a
two-way audio-visual platform. The current equipment cannot support this required functionality.




2025-11-19                               Item #08G                              Page 2 of 38

The simultaneous need to replace equipment and to comply with SB 707 requires a
comprehensive technology upgrade across all three meeting spaces. Ensuring the replacement
and integration of equipment across these rooms is necessary to minimize potential downtime in
the event of software or hardware failure in the future. Having overflow rooms equipped with
similar technology will help restore functionality for a two-way audio-visual platform to comply with
SB 707.

The Poinsettia Room, functions as the City's Emergency Operations Center (EOC). Hybrid
meeting capability in this room may be required for SB 707 compliance for any public meetings
held and for maintaining necessary communication infrastructure for EOC activation. The project
scope encompasses replacing and upgrading equipment in all three rooms to achieve the
reliability and functionality necessary to meet these technical and legal requirements.


ANALYSIS:

The primary driver is the need to upgrade AV equipment in support of SB 707 along with broadcast
equipment set to reach end of life in 2026. This proactive replacement mitigates the risk of sudden
system failure, ensuring operational continuity for all civic meetings.

All three rooms: Council Chambers, Poinsettia Room, and the Carnation Room, will receive full
hybrid meeting capabilities. This ensures flexibility and redundancy, allowing public meetings to
be conducted with hybrid participation as needed.

A core improvement is adding networked control for in-chambers equipment to be available via
software for broadcast technicians within our AV Control Room. This will streamline the broadcast
team's operations and avoid unnecessary interruptions related to fixable broadcast issues. This
modernization simplifies the IT workflow for setting up, controlling, and troubleshooting complex
meeting functions.

Pursuant to a Request for Proposal on January 10, 2020, the City received proposals from three
(3) consulting firms to upgrade the City’s audio-visual equipment at the locations above. Based
on several criteria including technical expertise, public sector experience and cost, staff selected
Western Audio Visual to perform the work which will include design, integration, hardware
installation, programming, testing, and project management. As such, Western Audio Visual will
be providing continuity of service by providing consistent design and maintenance of the audio-
visual systems detailed.

      AV upgrades from Western Audio Visual

Repaired beach condition at the Cardiff State Beach Living Shoreline 2025

On February 14, 2024, City Council authorized staff to apply for the SCC grant in order to continue
maintenance, monitoring, and permitting efforts for the project. On February 20, 2024, City staff
applied for the grant and on November 21, 2024, the SCC approved the City’s grant request
unanimously.
On February 12, 2025, City Council accepted the grant in the amount of $1,060,000 from the
SCC. The SCC grant will fund re-permitting and continued monitoring and maintenance of the
Cardiff State Beach Living Shoreline dune system for the next five years. The SCC approved
grant work plan is contained in Attachment 5. This work plan includes work from GHD Inc.,
Nature Collective, UCLA and State Parks. The grant project scope includes:

    1. Renew Coastal Development Permit Nos. 6-17-0596, 6-17-05961A and 6-17-059612A;
    2. Maintain approximately four acres of sand dunes that are heterogeneous in structure (i.e.
       incorporate cobble and sand) with a planted base of native dune plant species to stabilize
       the surface;
    3. Maintain sand dunes that will persist dynamically for approximately 50 years. Future
       maintenance may be required in the way of additional beach nourishment and active
       planting. Future maintenance work will be reviewed and permitted separately prior to
       commencement of the repair work;
    4. Beneficially reuse native beach quality sand from the San Elijo Lagoon and the City’s
       Opportunistic Beach Fill Program (OBFP) to construct and maintain the beach and dune
       system; and
    5. Continue to protect South Coast Highway 101 from its current vulnerability to episodic
       flooding and undermining.

On March 12, 2025, SCC finalized the Work Program for the granted project (Attachment 5). The
work program includes tasks assigned to GHD Inc., Nature Collective, UCLA, and State Parks.

ANALYSIS:

Sole source Professional Services Agreements with GHD, Inc. and Nature Collective are
necessary to support the fulfillment of tasks specified for these parties in the original MOA
(Attachment 4) and the grant’s Work Program (Attachment 5).

State Parks, Nature Collective, GHD, Inc., UCLA (subconsultant to nature Collective) and the City
of Encinitas have all been a part of the construction, maintenance, and monitoring effort of the
Cardiff State Beach Living Shoreline since initial construction finished in 2018. Over the last five
years, post-construction maintenance, monitoring, and reporting efforts have been conducted
annually, showing how the dune has performed in each respective year through winter storms
and spring maintenance efforts. Attachment 6 includes the final monitoring plan for the first five
years, showing the overall performance of the project as a living shoreline system.

Because of the success of this project, coastal management professionals as well as state and
federal agencies, nationwide, have been learning how to create other similar projects in areas
around the state, region and the coastal United States. Projects designed similar to the Cardiff
Living Shoreline can provide both a naturalized solution and an adequate buffer to ocean-adjacent
infrastructure, minimizing the impact of storm surge and wave action, as it relates to climate
change and sea level rise.

SCC’s approval of an additional five-year grant demonstrates their interest to continue
maintenance, monitoring, and permitting efforts for the project. Maintenance and monitoring
conducted for this project over the next five years, will enable the State of California and the nation
as a whole an opportunity to learn how to best manage our coastlines with non-invasive, nature-
based infrastructure, and will enable the City to continue to attenuate coastal damage related to
storm surge and sea level rise in the Cardiff State Beach area.

The City of Encinitas information technology platform is currently standardized on HP computer

goods by leveraging the purchasing power of public agencies nationally. NCPA utilizes state-of-
the-art procurement resources, which result in cooperative purchasing contracts that ensure
public agencies receive products of the highest quality at the lowest prices.

Staff recommends purchasing HP hardware in FY 2024-25 using the cooperative agreement.
Replacement of hardware when it has become obsolete is critical to cybersecurity. HP provides
patches and updates to maintain hardware security during the product lifecycle, recommending
hardware replacement at the end of its useful life. Using guidelines from agencies such as IEEE,
IT can proactively prepare for the replacement of end-of-life hardware. It helps avoid security
risks, lowered productivity, increased downtime, and elevated staff support that is associated with
older hardware.

RECOMMENDED ACTION:

   1. Authorize the City Manager, or designee, in consultation with the City Attorney, to execute

   2. Approve the sole source for design professional consultant services with Ardurra Group,

ENVIRONMENTAL CONSIDERATIONS:

The action being considered by the City Council is exempt from the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) because it is not a “project” under Section 15378(b)(5) of CEQA Guidelines.
The action involves an organizational or administrative activity of government that will not result
in the direct or indirect physical change in the environment.

This item is not related to the Climate Action Plan.

STRATEGIC PLAN:

The project aligns with the focus areas of Effective City Services & Reliable Infrastructure and
Environmental Health & Leadership vision of the FY 2024-25 Strategic Plan by providing
wastewater management through well-maintained infrastructure.




2024-06-26                                Item #08G                              Page 1 of 30

FISCAL CONSIDERATIONS:

The total cost of this agreement is $474,807 plus a ten percent (10%) contingency of $47,481 for
a not-to-exceed contract total of $522,288. There are sufficient funds in the Olivenhain Trunk
Sewer project (Project No. CC04J) to fund this agreement. There is no fiscal impact to the General
Fund.

BACKGROUND:

The City of Encinitas (“City”) owns and operates a wastewater collection system consisting of
approximately 126 miles of wastewater pipelines in the Encinitas and Cardiff Sanitary Divisions
which together serve a population of approximately 37,000 residents. There are approximately
121 miles of gravity sewers and five (5) miles of force mains.

The Olivenhain Trunk Sewer (OTS) is an existing 15-inch sewer line that runs nearly five (5) miles
along Escondido Creek and San Elijo Lagoon from Lone Jack Road to the Olivenhain Sewer
Pump Station located at the Manchester Ave./I-5 Interchange. The OTS was constructed 49 years
ago and is the City’s largest sewer pipeline. Rehabilitation of the OTS was identified as a high
priority project in the Sewer Master Plan Update approved by City Council on June 15, 2011. All
the pipe segments as well as their associated manholes need rehabilitation and/or replacement.
Additionally, there is a need to improve access to the trunk sewer and manholes for maintenance
purposes.

Improving the entire limits of OTS is a large undertaking and has been broken down into
manageable phases. Phases 1 and 1A were constructed in 2021 and 2023, respectively, and
these phases included upsizing the sewer along Lone Jack Road, removing approximately 1,100
feet of sewer out of the Escondido Creek and into the paved roadway, and rehabilitating a total of
51 manholes.

This phase, Phase 1B, will rehabilitate the remaining 19 manholes along the OTS system as well
as remove the siphon located within the system. Approval of this action will allow Ardurra to
complete the environmental permitting, engineering design, and right-of-way tasks necessary to
produce construction documents for Phase 1B. Future phases of the project will include
rehabilitating and/or replacing the sewer pipeline throughout the trunk sewer system.

On November 29, 2017, City Council awarded a design contract in the amount of $218,118 to
Infrastructure Engineering Corporation (IEC), which has since had a name change and is now
Ardurra Group, Inc., to finish preparing all required environmental documents, obtain all required
environmental permits, perform construction storm water monitoring, design plans, specifications,
and cost estimate for sewer improvements along the Olivenhain Trunk Sewer.

On June 13, 2018, City Council approved Amendment #1 in the amount of $413,115 for additional
work created after regulatory agency review of the project.

On January 16, 2019, City Council approved Amendment #2 in the amount of $139,544 for
additional work required by regulatory agencies and for design changes.

On August 21, 2019, City Council approved Amendment #3 in the amount of $64,160 for
additional work required by regulatory agencies and pursuing right-of-way negotiations.




2024-06-26                               Item #08G                              Page 2 of 30

On January 22, 2020, City Council approved Amendment #4 in the amount of $407,192 for
additional design and permitting services required by regulatory agencies.

On January 27, 2021, City Council approved Amendment #5 in the amount of $617,988 for
additional design, permitting, and right-of-way services due to regulatory agency and private
property owner requests and professional environmental and engineering services during
construction for Phase 1.

On March 1, 2022, City Council approved Amendment #6 in the amount of $155,400 for biological
services and engineering design services during construction for Phase 1A.

On November 28, 2022, City Council approved Amendment #7 which extended the duration of
the agreement through December 31, 2023, with no additional compensation allotted.

On December 31, 2023, the agreement with IEC/Ardurra expired.

ANALYSIS:

Ardurra, formerly IEC, has been providing environmental, engineering, permitting, right-of-way
support, and construction support services to the City for OTS for the past 13 years. They were
selected as the most highly qualified professional services firm to provide these services for the
OTS Improvements project and have aided the City in completing the project’s Environmental
Impact Report (for all phases of the project) and resource agency permits, engineering
construction plans, and right-of-way services for Phases 1 and 1A of the project. Ardurra
possesses intricate knowledge of the site constraints, technical expertise of the project elements,
and appropriate resources to efficiently complete the professional services effort for Phase 1B.
Refer to Attachment 2 for a detailed explanation of the sole source justification.

Construction was completed for Phase 1 in 2021 and Phase 1A in early 2023. Phase 1B, which
has professional design services within this agreement, includes the design plans, jurisdictional
agency permits, and right-of-way acquisition activities. These tasks must be completed prior to
requesting City Council to advertise Phase 1B work for construction The following services are
needed to continue working with regulatory agencies and complete easement acquisitions:

   •   Environmental services to complete biological surveys and coordinate jurisdictional
       agency permits.
   •   Engineering services to finalize the design plans.
   •   Right-of-way coordination services to obtain permits and authorizations to enter private
       parcels during construction:

In 2011, after conducting interviews with short-listed consultants, Ardurra (then called

FISCAL CONSIDERATIONS:

The fiscal impact of $55,300 is included in the approved Fiscal Year 2023-24 budget. Funding in

BACKGROUND:

On November 22, 2023, the City entered into a three-year agreement with Control Air Enterprises,
LLC (Control Air) for maintenance and repair of Automated Logic (ALC) HVAC control systems at
City facilities for a total agreement amount not-to-exceed $71,218 (Attachment 2). The
agreement, as amended, is effective through December 31, 2026.

The services provided under the agreement consist of quarterly maintenance and inspection of
HVAC controls at the City Hall, Public Works, Community Senior Center, and Library facilities.
The controls enable staff and Control Air to remotely monitor, troubleshoot, and schedule HVAC
equipment at these facilities. Staff is also alerted when systems malfunction. In addition to
quarterly maintenance and inspection, Control Air performs non-routine repairs, equipment
replacement and installation of new systems that are not included in the basic scope of services
on a case-by-case basis.

On January 24, 2024, the City Council approved funding in the amount of $20,000 for HVAC
controls at the Pacific View Arts Center.

ANALYSIS:

In order to provide the same benefits noted above for the Pacific View Arts Center, Control Air
has proposed integrating the Pacific View HVAC system into the City’s existing controls. Due to
the variety of events and classes held at Pacific View, settings and schedules for the HVAC
system will vary. By having remote access, facilities staff will be able to make adjustments and
respond to any system alerts in a timely manner. The cost of installation of controls at Pacific
View is $19,500.

The controls at City Hall currently only enable staff to monitor, schedule and troubleshoot the
settings for heating and cooling of the building. The system is in need of an upgrade to integrate
the generator and boiler into the controls to provide an additional layer of monitoring and alerts
for staff for any issues that may impact these two (2) critical components. The cost of integrating
the generator and boiler into the existing system is $5,400.

During a recent upgrade to the City Hall controls to provide the most current version of the ALC
system, several parts of the existing system were discovered to be non-operable and obsolete.
These parts are in need of replacement to be compatible with the current ALC system. The cost
of replacing these parts is $5,400.

In addition to installing controls at Pacific View and upgrading the City Hall system, staff
recommends adding $25,000 to the agreement not-to-exceed amount for unforeseen, as-needed
repairs which are not covered under the standard maintenance agreement over the life of the
agreement. If approved by the City Council, the total amended not-to-exceed agreement amount
will be $126,518.

                        5.3 Flashing Stop Signs
Studies have shown that flashing stop signs provide significant beneficial effects on daytime
and nighttime stopping compliance and are effective in reducing stop sign violations. The
2014 California Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (CA MUTCD), Section 2A.07 (or
the most recent relevant section) provides standards and options for the usage of Light
Emitting Diode (LED) units within the face of a sign and in the border of a sign to improve
conspicuity and increase the legibility of sign legends and borders. This policy outlines the
requirements that must be met for a flashing LED stop sign to be installed at City of Encinitas
maintained intersections.
POLICY
Installation of a flashing LED stop sign can be considered by the City Traffic Engineer at
locations that meet at least 3 out of 5 criteria below. City Traffic Engineer may implement
LED stop signs at any stop-controlled intersection if staff evaluation finds it beneficial.
   1. At least 3 susceptible to correction collisions during last 12 months
   2. Located within ½ mile of school, park, or other major pedestrian generator
   3. At least 30 pedestrians/bikes crossing study approaches during the peak 15-min

Diegan coastal sage scrub–Baccharis-dominated is similar to Diegan coastal sage scrub but is dominated by
Baccharis species (desertbroom [B. sarothroides] and/or coyote brush) (Oberbauer et al. 2008). This community
typically occurs on disturbed sites or those with nutrient-poor soils and is often found within other forms of Diegan
coastal sage scrub and on upper terraces of river valleys. This community is distributed along coastal and foothill
areas in San Diego County. On site, the Diegan coastal sage scrub–Baccharis-dominated vegetation community is
dominated by coyote brush, with relatively low cover of California buckwheat, California sagebrush, Menzies’
goldenbush (Isocoma menziesii var. vernonioides), and western ragweed (Ambrosia psilostachya), along with
non-native perennial veldtgrass and hottentot fig (Carpobrotus edulis). There is 0.54 acres of Diegan coastal sage
scrub–Baccharis-dominated within the Lake Drive project site, as shown in Figure 5A.


3.1.3           Non-native Grassland
Non-native grassland consists of dense to sparse cover of annual grasses, with flowering culms 0.5 feet to 3 feet
in height (Oberbauer et al. 2008). In some areas, depending on past disturbance and annual rainfall, annual forbs
may be the dominant species; however, it is presumed that grasses will dominate.

Non-native grassland on site is dominated by perennial veldtgrass; this area had been treated at the time of
mapping. A much smaller portion of non-native grassland consists of mowed lawn on the edge of the Lake Drive
project site. There is 0.14 acres of non-native grassland within the Lake Drive project site, located along the
southern boundary (Figure 5A).


3.1.4           Disturbed Habitat
Disturbed habitat contains predominantly non-native and/or weedy species that indicate disturbance and soil
compaction, such as Russian thistle (Salsola tragus), telegraphweed (Heterotheca grandiflora), horehound
(Marrubium vulgare), and sowthistle (Sonchus oleraceus). In areas with less than 10% vegetative cover, there is
evidence of soil surface disturbance and compaction. In areas with higher vegetative cover, there is soil surface
disturbance and compaction, and the presence of building foundations and debris.

Disturbed land within the Lake Drive project site (0.07 acres) is located within the southeastern corner of the Lake
Drive project site and appears to be a historical dirt road (Figure 5A).


3.1.5           Eucalyptus Woodland
Oberbauer et al. (2008) describes eucalyptus woodland as a non-native vegetation type that is fairly widespread in
Southern California. It typically consists of monotypic stands of introduced Australian eucalyptus trees (Eucalyptus
spp.). The understory is either poor or lacking, owing to shade and possible allelopathic (toxic) properties of the
eucalyptus leaf litter. Although eucalyptus woodlands are of limited value to most native plants and animals, they
frequently provide nesting and perching sites for some raptors.

Eucalyptus woodland within the Lake Drive project site (0.73 acres) occurs adjacent to the residential development
along the outer boundary of the Lake Drive project site, as shown in Figure 5A. These areas contain Bald Island
marlock (Eucalyptus conferruminata) and red ironbark (Eucalyptus sideroxylon).

3.1.6             Urban/Developed
Urban/developed refers to areas that have been constructed on or disturbed so severely that native vegetation is

The 0.14-acre Manchester Avenue project site consists of open water, coastal and valley freshwater marsh, and

Manchester Avenue project site contains three vegetation communities and/or land cover types. The vegetation
communities and land cover types recorded on the Manchester Avenue project site are described in detail below,
their acreages are presented in Table 3, and their spatial distributions are presented in Figure 5B, Manchester

Sensitive habitats are those that are considered rare within the region or support special-status plant and/or wildlife

3.2.2            Coastal and Valley Freshwater Marsh
Coastal and valley freshwater marsh is a wetland habitat that is permanently flooded by fresh water lacking a
significant current (Oberbauer et al. 2008). Because it is permanently flooded by fresh water, there is an
accumulation of deep, peaty soils. This vegetation community is typically dominated by species such as cattail
(Typha spp.), sedge (Carex spp.), yellow nutsedge (Cyperus esculentus), and bulrushes (Scirpus spp.).

The coastal and valley freshwater marsh covers 0.05 acres of the Manchester Avenue project site and is dominated
by southern cattail (Typha domingensis) with a few scattered arroyo willows (Salix lasiolepis) (Figure 5B). This
community has regrown since the emergency sediment removal occurred in December 2020.


3.2.3            Disturbed Habitat
Disturbed habitats are areas that have been physically disturbed and are no longer recognizable as a native or
naturalized vegetation association (Oberbauer et al. 2008). These areas may continue to retain soil substrate. If
vegetation is present, it is almost entirely composed of non-native vegetation, such as ornamentals or ruderal exotic
species. Examples of these areas may include graded landscapes or areas, graded firebreaks, graded construction
pads, temporary construction staging areas, off-road-vehicle trails, areas repeatedly cleared for fuel management,
or areas that are repeatedly used in ways that prevent revegetation (e.g., parking lots, trails that have persisted for
years) (Oberbauer et al. 2008).

Within the Manchester Avenue project site, 0.08 acres of disturbed habitat occurs between the culvert outfall head
wall and Manchester Avenue (Figure 5B). The disturbed habitat area has compacted soils and very limited
vegetation and was used as the staging area during the December 2020 emergency excavation work.


3.3              Floral Diversity
A total of 164 vascular plant species, 104 (63%) native and 60 (37%) non-native species, were recorded during the
biological reconnaissance surveys for the Lake Drive project site. A cumulative list of all common and sensitive
plant species observed on the Lake Drive project site is provided in Appendix A1. A total of 12 vascular plant species,
10 (83%) native and 2 (17%) non-native species, were recorded during the biological reconnaissance surveys for
the Manchester Avenue project site. A cumulative list of all common and sensitive plant species observed on the
Manchester Avenue project site is provided in Appendix A2.


3.4              Wildlife Diversity
The Lake Drive project site supports habitat primarily for upland wildlife species, whereas the Manchester Avenue
project site provides habitat for riparian wildlife species. These habitat types provide foraging and nesting habitat
for migratory and resident bird species and other wildlife species.

As noted in Section 2.2, wildlife species that were detected during the field survey by sight, calls, tracks, scat, or
other signs were recorded directly in a field notebook or using an electronic form on a mobile device. Binoculars
(10 × 42 magnification) were used to aid in the identification of wildlife. A total of 40 wildlife species were recorded
during wildlife surveys on the Lake Drive project site, consisting of 2 butterfly species, 2 reptile species, 30 bird
species, and 6 mammal species. A cumulative list of wildlife species observed in the Lake Drive project site during
field surveys is provided in Appendix B1. A total of 4 wildlife species were recorded during wildlife surveys on the
Manchester Avenue project site, consisting of 4 bird species. A cumulative list of wildlife species observed in the
Manchester Avenue project site during field surveys is provided in Appendix B2.


3.4.1            Amphibians and Reptiles
No amphibians were observed during the wildlife surveys in either site. Two reptile species, western fence lizard
(Sceloporus occidentalis) and common side-blotched lizard (Uta stansburiana), were observed during surveys within
the Lake Drive project site. No reptile species were observed within the Manchester Avenue project site.


3.4.2            Birds
There were 30 species of birds observed during the surveys within the Lake Drive project site. Birds adapted to
human disturbance, such as mourning dove (Zenaida macroura), northern mockingbird (Mimus polyglottos),
common raven (Corvus corax), and Anna’s hummingbird (Calypte anna), were observed, as well as species
associated with scrub or chaparral habitats, such as coastal California gnatcatcher and Southern California rufous-
crowned sparrow (Aimophila ruficeps canescens). Flying or foraging birds observed were red-tailed hawk (Buteo
jamaicensis) and Cooper’s hawk (Accipiter cooperii). Four bird species were observed during surveys within the
Manchester Avenue project site including bushtit (Psaltriparus minimus), black phoebe (Sayornis nigricans),
common yellowthroat (Geothlypis trichas), and yellow-rumped warbler (Setophaga coronata).


3.4.3            Mammals
Four common mammal species were detected within the Lake Drive project site: brush rabbit (Sylvilagus bachmani),
California ground squirrel (Otospermophilus beecheyi), California deermouse (Peromyscus californicus), and desert
cottontail (Sylvilagus audubonii). Two special-status species were observed during the small mammal live capture
surveys: San Diego desert woodrat (Neotoma lepida intermedia) and northwestern San Diego pocket mouse
(Chaetodipus fallax fallax). Other human-adapted species, such as Botta’s pocket gopher (Thomomys bottae),
northern racoon (Procyon lotor), and striped skunk (Mephitis mephitis), are likely to use the area. No mammal
species were observed within the Manchester Avenue project site.


3.5              Special-Status Plants
Plant species are considered special status if they have been listed or proposed for listing by the federal or state
government as rare, endangered, or threatened (“listed species”), are covered under the draft Encinitas Subarea Plan
(City of Encinitas 2001), and/or have a CRPR of 1 or 2. An evaluation of known records in the Encinitas quadrangle
and the surrounding quadrangles (CDFW 2021; CNPS 2022; USFWS 2021a) was conducted to determine which
species have been recorded in the project vicinity. In addition, Dudek biologists’ knowledge of biological resources,

3.5.1            Lake Drive Project Site
Seven sensitive plant species—Campbell’s liverwort (Geothallus tuberosus), Del Mar Mesa sand aster, Nuttall’s
scrub oak, Torrey pine, San Diego barrel cactus (Ferocactus viridescens), wart-stemmed ceanothus, and sea
dahlia—were observed naturally occurring within the Lake Drive project site during the 2021 and 2022 survey effort.
Locations of special-status plants are shown in Figure 5A.

Campbell’s liverwort, a CRPR 1B.1 species, is an ephemeral liverwort that occurs in mesic coastal scrub and vernal
pools (CNPS 2022). It occurs in Riverside and San Diego Counties (CNPS 2022). There are at least 17 locations of
Campbell’s liverwort throughout the Lake Drive project site. Each location in Figure 5A represents a patch or cluster
of patches.

Del Mar Mesa sand aster, a CRPR 1B.1 and narrow endemic species under the draft Encinitas Subarea Plan, is a
perennial herb that occurs in sandy coastal bluff scrub, maritime chaparral, and coastal scrub (City of Encinitas
2001; CNPS 2022). It occurs in coastal regions from Encinitas south to Torrey Pines (CCH 2021). The Lake Drive
project site overlaps a major population area of Del Mar Mesa sand aster, as recognized by the MHCP, but does
not include any critical locations of this variety (SANDAG 2003). Approximately 194 individuals of Del Mar Mesa
sand aster were observed in the southern, northern, and central portions of the Lake Drive project site.

Nuttall’s scrub oak, a CRPR 1B.1 and covered species under the draft Encinitas Subarea Plan, is a perennial
evergreen shrub that occurs in sandy or clay loam soils in closed-cone coniferous forest, chaparral, and coastal
scrub habitats from Santa Barbara County south to San Diego County (City of Encinitas 2001; CNPS 2022). The
project site does not contain any major population areas or critical locations of this species (SANDAG 2003). There
were 10 individuals of Nuttall’s scrub oak observed in the southern maritime chaparral in the northwestern portion
of the Lake Drive project site.

Torrey pine, a CRPR 1B.2 and covered species under the draft Encinitas Subarea Plan, is a perennial evergreen
tree that occurs in sandstone in closed-cone coniferous forest and chaparral habitats and is endemic to San Diego
County (City of Encinitas 2001; CNPS 2022). The Lake Drive project site does not contain any major population
areas or critical locations of this species (SANDAG 2003). Six individuals of Torrey pine, including one immature
individual and one individual in poor health, were observed in the southern maritime chaparral and Diegan coastal
sage scrub in the western and eastern portions of the Lake Drive project site.

San Diego barrel cactus, a CRPR 2B.1 and covered species under the draft Encinitas Subarea Plan, is a perennial
stem succulent that occurs in chaparral, coastal scrub, valley and foothill grassland, and vernal pools and is
endemic to San Diego County (City of Encinitas 2001; CNPS 2022). The project site does not contain any major
population areas or critical locations of this species (SANDAG 2003). A total of 43 individuals of San Diego barrel
cactus were observed, primarily in the southern portion of the Lake Drive project site.

Wart-stemmed ceanothus, a CRPR 2B.2 and covered species under the draft Encinitas Subarea Plan, is a perennial
evergreen shrub that occurs in chaparral (City of Encinitas 2001; CNPS 2022). It generally occurs in coastal regions
from Carlsbad south to Point Loma (CCH 2021). The project site does not contain any major population areas or

LAKE DRIVE STORM DRAIN PROJECT, CITY OF ENCINITAS, CALIFORNIA / UPLANDS HABITAT MITIGATION
AND MONITORING PLAN



On site, southern maritime chaparral was characterized by dominance or co-dominance of wart-stemmed
ceanothus, chamise, Nuttall’s scrub oak, Mohave yucca, mission manzanita, and Del Mar Mesa sand aster. A few
Torrey pines are also present within this community on site. Southern maritime chaparral tends to intergrade with
Diegan coastal sage scrub on site, so lesser cover of species typically associated with coastal sage scrub, such as
lemonade berry (Rhus integrifolia), black sage (Salvia mellifera), California sagebrush (Artemisia californica), laurel
sumac, coast prickly pear (Opuntia littoralis), and coyote brush (Baccharis pilularis), were also present in areas
mapped as southern maritime chaparral. Some areas were disturbed by the presence of perennial veldtgrass
(Ehrharta calycina). The project site contains 6.56 acres of southern maritime chaparral (Figure 4).

Diegan Coastal Sage Scrub (Including Baccharis-Dominated and Restored/Landscaped)

Diegan coastal sage scrub is a native vegetation community. According to Oberbauer et al. (2008), coastal sage
scrub is composed of a variety of soft, low, aromatic shrubs, characteristically dominated by drought-deciduous
species—such as California sagebrush, California buckwheat (Eriogonum fasciculatum), and sages (Salvia spp.)—
with scattered evergreen shrubs, including lemonade berry and laurel sumac.

Diegan coastal sage scrub covers 16.49 acres of the project site. The Diegan coastal sage scrub on site is
dominated by California buckwheat, California brittle bush (Encelia californica), lemonade berry, black sage (Salvia
mellifera), and/or California sagebrush. Other associated species include common deerweed (Acmispon glaber var.
glaber), laurel sumac, red bush monkeyflower (Diplacus puniceus), and rod wirelettuce (Stephanomeria virgata ssp.
Virgata). Low cover of species generally associated with chaparral, such as chamise, chaparral yucca
(Hesperoyucca whipplei), and Mohave yucca, were present in some areas mapped as Diegan coastal sage scrub.
Portions of the Diegan coastal sage scrub on the project site were disturbed by high cover of perennial veldtgrass.

In addition, 0.17 acres of the project site contains Diegan coastal sage scrub that has been restored/landscaped
by The Nature Collective. This area is mapped as restored/landscaped Diegan coastal sage scrub. This area
includes several species that, when occurring naturally, have special-status designations, including Shaw’s agave
(Agave shawii var. shawii), golden-spined cereus (Bergerocactus emoryi), cliff spurge (Euphorbia misera), and red-
flowered buckwheat (Eriogonum grande var. rubescens). None of these species were observed in the natural areas
of the project site.

Diegan coastal sage scrub–Baccharis-dominated is similar to Diegan coastal sage scrub but is dominated by
Baccharis species (desert broom [B. sarothroides] and/or coyote brush) (Oberbauer et al. 2008). This community
typically occurs on disturbed sites or those with nutrient-poor soils, and is often found within other forms of Diegan
coastal sage scrub and on upper terraces of river valleys. This community is distributed along coastal and foothills
areas in San Diego County.

On site the Diegan coastal sage scrub–Baccharis-dominated is dominated by coyote brush, with relatively low cover
of California buckwheat, California sagebrush, Menzies’ goldenbush (Isocoma menziesii var. vernonioides), and
western ragweed (Ambrosia psilostachya), along with non-native perennial veldtgrass and hottentot fig
(Carpobrotus edulis). There is 0.54 acres of Diegan coastal sage scrub–Baccharis-dominated within the project site
(Figure 4).

Eucalyptus Woodland

Oberbauer et al. (2008) describes eucalyptus woodland as a non-native vegetation type that is fairly widespread in
Southern California. It typically consists of monotypic stands of introduced Australian eucalyptus trees (Eucalyptus

eucalyptus leaf litter. Although eucalyptus woodlands are of limited value to most native plants and animals, they

Eucalyptus woodland within the project site (0.82 acres) occurs adjacent to the residential development along the

conferruminata) and red ironbark (Eucalyptus sideroxylon).

Urban/Developed

Urban/developed refers to areas that have been constructed on or disturbed so severely that native vegetation is
no longer supported. Urban/developed land includes areas with permanent or semi-permanent structures,
pavement or hardscape, landscaped areas, and areas with a large amount of debris or other materials (Oberbauer
et al. 2008). Urban/developed land within the project site (0.64 acres) includes paved roads and portions of the
residential homes adjacent to the project site (Figure 4).


2.3             Special-Status Plant Species
Seven sensitive plant species—Campbell’s liverwort, Del Mar Mesa sand aster, Nuttall’s scrub oak, Torrey pine, San
Diego barrel cactus (Ferocactus viridescens), wart-stemmed ceanothus, and sea dahlia—were observed naturally
occurring within the project site during the 2021 and 2022 survey effort (Figure 4). Of the seven special-status
species observed, five would be directly impacted by the proposed project, excluding Nuttall’s scrub oak and San
Diego barrel cactus. All special-status species will be avoided to the maximum extent feasible.

Shaw’s agave, golden-spined cereus, red-flowered buckwheat, and cliff spurge were observed planted in the
restored/landscaped Diegan coastal sage scrub along Lake Drive on site. Direct impacts would occur to planted
Shaw’s agave and golden-spined cereus; however, because these species were planted outside of their native
range, impacts to these individuals would be less than significant and are therefore not included in this HMMP.

Campbell’s liverwort, a California Rare Plant Rank (CRPR) 1B.1 species, is an ephemeral liverwort that occurs in
mesic coastal scrub and vernal pools (CNPS 2024). It occurs in Riverside and San Diego Counties (CNPS 2024).
There are at least 17 locations of Campbell’s liverwort throughout the project site. Each location in Figure 4
represents a patch or cluster of patches.

Del Mar Mesa sand aster, a CRPR 1B.1 and narrow endemic species under the draft Encinitas Subarea Plan, is a
perennial herb that occurs in sandy coastal bluff scrub, maritime chaparral, and coastal scrub (City of Encinitas
2001; CNPS 2024). It occurs in coastal regions from Encinitas south to Torrey Pines (CCH 2024). The project site
overlaps a major population area of Del Mar Mesa sand aster, as recognized by the MHCP, but does not include
any critical locations of this variety (SANDAG 2003). Approximately 194 individuals of Del Mar Mesa sand aster
were observed in the southern, northern, and central portions of the project site.

Nuttall’s scrub oak, a CRPR 1B.1 and covered species under the draft Encinitas Subarea Plan, is a perennial
evergreen shrub that occurs in sandy or clay loam soils in closed-cone conifer forest, chaparral, and coastal scrub
habitats from Santa Barbara County south to San Diego County (City of Encinitas 2001; CNPS 2024). The project
site does not contain any major population areas or critical locations of this species (SANDAG 2003). There were

observed throughout the Lake Drive project site, primarily in southern maritime chaparral.

Sea dahlia, a CRPR 2B.2 species, is a perennial herb that occurs in coastal bluff scrub and coastal scrub (City of
Encinitas 2001; CNPS 2024). In California, it primarily occurs in coastal regions from Camp Pendleton south to
Border Field State Park, but there is a record as far north as Rancho Palos Verde and as far east as Potrero (CCH

3                Proposed Mitigation Design Approach
See Section 1.4, Mitigation Goals and Objectives, for a summary of project impacts, mitigation ratio requirements,
special-status plant species, and proposed mitigation.


3.1              Enhancement/Restoration Mitigation
Proposed mitigation for 2.40 acres of permanent impacts to sensitive vegetation communities includes 0.79 acres of
southern maritime chaparral enhancement (to compensate for 0.26 acres of impacts) and 4.28 acres of Diegan coastal
sage scrub (Coastal Form) enhancement (to compensate for 1.97 acres of impacts and 0.16 acres of impacts to
Baccharis-dominated Diegan coastal sage scrub). Permanent impact mitigation is proposed within the southwestern
portion of the project site within disturbed southern maritime chaparral and Diegan coastal sage scrub habitat (Figure 5,
Uplands Mitigation Plan). These areas were identified during baseline surveys and site assessment, as well as by The
Nature Collective, as disturbed habitat areas due to the non-native cover existing within these areas, dominated by
perennial veldtgrass and hottentot fig. Enhancement would include removal of non-native species and subsequent
planting and seeding of native species. Non-native species requiring removal include (but are not limited to) perennial
veldtgrass, hottentot fig, fountain grass (Pennisetum setaceum), eucalyptus (seedlings), acacia (Acacia redolens, A.
cyclops), and tree tobacco (Nicotiana glauca). All native species will be avoided and preserved during all enhancement
activities. A 5-year maintenance and monitoring program is proposed for all mitigation areas.

Proposed mitigation for 1 acre of temporary impacts will include restoration of temporary impact areas at a 1:1
ratio, including 0.70 acres of Diegan coastal sage scrub (Coastal Form), 0.05 acres of Diegan coastal sage scrub
(Baccharis-dominated), and 0.25 acres of southern maritime chaparral (Figure 5). Restoration is proposed through
planting and seeding of native vegetation communities and implementation of a 5-year maintenance and
monitoring program. Additionally, 0.06 acres of temporary impacts to non-native vegetation and land covers will be
revegetated with an erosion control seed mix for stabilization purposes (Figure 5). Erosion control areas are
proposed to include a 2-year maintenance and monitoring program to ensure successful stabilization of these
temporary impact areas.


3.2              Special-Status Plant Species Mitigation
Proposed mitigation for impacts to special-status plant species includes flagging all special-status individuals within
the impact footprint and a 20-foot buffer by a qualified biologist prior to construction activities. If avoidance is not
possible, impacts to each special-status species will be documented and individuals either translocated, planted,
or seeded on site outside of the project impact footprint (see Section 1.4). Translocation sites will be permanently
conserved locations of suitable habitat that are determined by the habitat restoration specialist and selected using
appropriate habitat factors (e.g., vegetation, soils, aspect, steepness) prior to construction. These locations will be
prepared prior to translocation (e.g., weeds removed, soil amended), if determined necessary by the habitat
restoration specialist. Seed and replacement plants will be sourced locally or from a reputable vendor.

3.2.1            Campbell’s Liverwort Mitigation Method
Campbell’s liverwort is a non-vascular plant species that grows low to the ground. If flagging and avoidance is not
possible, but impacts would be limited to trampling or other disturbance that does not require removal of the soil,

Campbell’s liverwort will be salvaged by removing the bryophyte along with its host soil (6 inches depth) and re-
establishing it outside the project’s impact footprint in a suitable location selected by the habitat restoration specialist.

If translocation of Campbell’s liverwort is determined necessary by the habitat restoration specialist, then the
liverwort will be salvaged during the dry season and planted before the first rain event of the winter season. The
translocated liverwort and soil patches will be lightly watered immediately following translocation to blend the soil
substrate into the receptor site to provide stabilization before the first rain event.


3.3              Mitigation Site Selection Criteria
Following analysis of existing baseline conditions and evaluation of on-site mitigation opportunities owned by The
Nature Collective, implementation of permittee-responsible mitigation on site was determined to be adequate to
meet the mitigation requirements, goals, and objectives of the project. The proposed mitigation locations provide
equal or improved functions as the pre-project condition of impacted resources. The selected mitigation locations
provide a net benefit because they support or have the potential to support “like” habitats in the project impact
area and will continue to be conserved and managed in perpetuity by The Nature Collective as City open space
following the completion of the mitigation program.

The enhancement areas were selected based on the high cover of non-native invasive species. Enhancement
activities within these areas will provide a net benefit to improve functions and services within those habitat types,
providing an increase of suitable habitat for sensitive species.

Receptor locations for significantly impacted special-status plant species will be on site but outside of the project’s
impact footprint and on The Nature Collective–owned land. Final receptor locations for each species will be
determined by the habitat restoration specialist.


3.4              Rationale for Expecting Project Success
The purpose for mitigation activities is to restore vegetation communities that were permanently and temporarily
impacted during project construction activities. All temporary impact areas are proposed to be restored in-place, in-
kind to pre-project conditions. The natural condition of these areas is the target community; therefore, the areas
proposed for temporary impact restoration are suitable for the proposed vegetation communities.

Permanent impacts are proposed to be mitigated within on-site vegetation communities, consistent with the
sensitive vegetation communities being impacted, through enhancement activities. There are established native
plant species suitable for southern maritime chaparral and Diegan coastal sage scrub vegetation communities,
showing health and vigor. However, the restoration areas were selected due to their high disturbance from non-
native species cover. Success is anticipated given the suitability of these areas (e.g., soils, slope, aspect, water
availability) to support the target vegetation communities, and the current presence of sensitive wildlife, such as
California gnatcatcher (Polioptila californica). A functional lift is anticipated within these areas due to proposed non-
native vegetation removal and native planting and seeding.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

The project is for a request to authorize a new Type 47 ABC license for a new restaurant
establishment, including outdoor patio dining areas totaling approximately 2,300 square feet, live
entertainment, and associated site improvements. The Type 47 ABC license authorizes the sale
of beer, wine and distilled spirits at a bona-fide eating establishment.

The project scope requires the following permit types:

   •   Minor Use Permit
          o Establish a new restaurant with a Type 47 ABC license.
          o Authorize alcohol sales in the expanded patio areas.
          o Allow live entertainment with indoor amplified music.
          o Parking study to demonstrate adequate parking supply.

   •   Design Review Permit

This tenant location was considered to have a legal non-conforming use since a use permit to
serve alcohol is required within this zone and none has existed since prior to the City of Encinitas
incorporation. City business records show that the tenant space has been used in the past by
various restaurant tenants with alcohol sales. ABC records indicate that the tenant space has held
a Type 41 ABC license for various restaurants since 1985. The most recent alcohol serving

(CW23C) to Cardiff Waterline Replacement Design and Engineering Services During
Construction, henceforth referred to as “Project”.

Water Infrastructure Improvements Project (CW23C) has unencumbered funds in the
approximate amount of $1,450,000.

The project will have expended approximately $126,105 from general Water Infrastructure
Improvements Project (CW23C). Staff is also requesting a budget transfer from project CW23C
to CW26E, to classify these capital expenses to the new project created (CW26E).

BACKGROUND:

As part of the District’s commitment to providing its customers with reliable potable water, the
District identified CIP projects in the 2022 Water System Master Plan (WSMP) to identify system
improvements that will provide reliable and efficient water service. The WSMP identified pipe
segments in the District’s system recommended for replacement due to condition.

The WSMP identified pipe segments NT-1 and NT-2 for replacement. Pipe segment NT-1 is
located in Liverpool Drive and the alley between Edinburg Avenue and Cambridge Avenue from
Liverpool Drive to Norfolk Drive. Pipe segment NT-2 is located in three alleys including the alley
between Manchester Avenue and Newcastle Avenue from Newcastle Avenue to Dublin Drive, the
alley between Montgomery Avenue and Manchester Avenue from Chesterfield Drive to Norfolk
Drive, and the alley between Oxford Avenue and Montgomery Avenue from Chesterfield Drive to
Dublin Drive. The pipe segment in the alley between Manchester Avenue and Newcastle Avenue
from Chesterfield Drive to Newcastle Avenue is included in the Project for replacement due to
pipe condition and proximity to segment NT-2. Refer to Attachment No. 3 for location information.

Dudek completed survey and 50 percent design of the Project through an as-needed professional
services agreement (Original Agreement) initiated in March 2021. The Original Agreement was
renewed in May 2024 and extended to March 2026. The Original Agreement cannot be renewed.

The Original Agreement with Dudek included the design of several critical projects. Due to the
complexity of these projects, delays occurred that impacted the Cardiff Pipeline Replacement
Project. Additionally, during the design phase of this project, it was determined that further
investigations were necessary, including geotechnical studies, alley resurfacing assessments,
utility conflict evaluations, and analysis of construction impacts on nearby residents.

Time is of the essence for this project, District staff recommend Dudek continues to work on the
Project with a project specific agreement. Dudek possesses intricate knowledge of the site
constraints in the alleys and appropriate resources to efficiently complete the design and provide
engineering services during construction. If the District were to hire a new engineering team, the
project schedule would extend by approximately 12 months due to the consultant selection
process, and the time it would take for the new consultant team to become familiar with the
intricate knowledge of the project elements. Also, a new consultant team would have to bear
additional costs for the work needed to become familiar with the project.

After careful consideration, District staff recommends a sole source project specific agreement
award to Dudek. Attachment No. 4 provides a detailed explanation of the sole source justification.
The scope of work includes completion of the design, support during the bid process, and
